Number theory

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics
OurBigBook.com Words: 63k Articles: 969
Number theory studies integers, their divisibility, and the patterns created by prime numbers. Its questions often have short statements but rigid answers: which integers divide a given one, when does an equation have integer solutions, and when can arithmetic with congruence classes be reversed? The Euclidean algorithm and modular multiplicative inverses connect these questions through explicit calculations.
For example, 252=22⋅32⋅7 and 198=2⋅32⋅11. Their shared prime factors give greatest common divisor 18. The Euclidean algorithm reaches that answer without finding either complete prime factorization. It also produces 18=4⋅252−5⋅198, an instance of Bézout's identity. This relation certifies every common divisor at once and solves an associated linear Diophantine equation.
Modular arithmetic retains only remainders, but the lost information can be surprisingly controlled. Multiplication by 5 modulo 17 is a permutation of all residue classes, because 5 has modular inverse 7. Multiplication by 5 modulo 15 collapses fifteen residue classes to three. Thus an apparently small change in the modulus changes whether a calculation can be reversed. The Chinese remainder theorem explains another kind of compression: remainders modulo coprime integers can be combined into one remainder modulo their product.
Simple restrictions help reveal the structure without telling the whole story. Every prime number greater than three is congruent to 1 or 5 modulo 6: the other four residue classes force divisibility by 2 or 3. The converse fails because 25 and 35 lie in those classes but are composite numbers. Necessary conditions are useful filters, not substitutes for primality testing.
The subject's appeal lies partly in this tension: prime factorization gives a clean description of every positive integer, while identifying factors and predicting their distribution lead to substantial further questions. Analytic number theory uses tools from analysis to study global patterns, and algebraic number theory extends arithmetic into number fields. Applications include cryptography and error-correcting codes; MIT's discrete applied mathematics course develops modular structures for both purposes. [ref]
Euclid's Elements already gives a greatest-common-measure construction in Book VII, Proposition 2, and the argument that a finite list cannot exhaust the prime numbers in Book IX, Proposition 20. These are documented ancient treatments, rather than evidence that all of number theory began with one author. [ref] [ref]

Sum of two squares

Words: 26
Number theory OurBigBook.com
A representation n=a2+b2 with integers a,b. Signs, ordering, and whether zero is allowed must be specified when counting representations. The sum of two squares theorem characterizes which nonnegative integers have such a representation.

Four exponentials conjecture

Number theory OurBigBook.com

Pronic number (n(n+1))

Words: 15
Number theory OurBigBook.com
A pronic number is the product n(n+1) of consecutive nonnegative integers. It is twice a triangular number.

Cube-full number

Words: 23
Number theory OurBigBook.com
A cube-full number is a positive integer in which every occurring prime factor has exponent at least three. The number 1 is included by the empty-product convention.

Jacobi's four-square theorem

Arithmetic derivative (n′)

Words: 31
Number theory OurBigBook.com
The arithmetic derivative on positive integers is defined by p′=1 for every prime p and the product rule (ab)′=a′b+ab′. For n=∏i​piei​​, these rules give n′=n∑i​ei​/pi​. In particular, (pe)′=epe−1.

Harshad number

Words: 47
Number theory OurBigBook.com
A Harshad number in base b≥2 is a positive integer divisible by its base-p digit sum in that base. In base ten, 18 is a Harshad number because 1+8=9 divides 18. It is strong when the quotient by its base-p digit sum is prime, and right-truncatable when every nonempty prefix is a Harshad number.

Frobenius number (g(a1​,…,ak​))

Words: 45 Articles: 1
Number theory OurBigBook.com
For positive integers a1​,…,ak​ with greatest common divisor 1, and with every ai​>1, the largest integer not expressible as a nonnegative integer linear combination of the ai​. For two coprime generators a,b, it equals ab−a−b.

Two-generator Frobenius theorem

Words: 15
Frobenius number OurBigBook.com
For coprime integers a,b>1, the Frobenius number is ab−a−b. Every larger integer is a nonnegative integer linear combination of a,b.

Practical number

Words: 32
Number theory OurBigBook.com
A positive integer n such that every positive integer at most n is a sum of distinct divisors of n. For example, 6 is practical because its divisors 1,2,3,6 represent every value from 1 through 6.

Product-sum number

Words: 58
Number theory OurBigBook.com
A positive integer N that is both the sum and the product of one multiset of k positive integers. For factors at least 2 with product P, sum S, and count t, appending P−S ones gives k=t+P−S without changing the product. For k≥2, the example 2,k with k−2 ones proves that the smallest product-sum value is at most 2k.

Integer factorization (N=∏p​pvp​(N))

Words: 1k Articles: 11
Number theory OurBigBook.com
Integer factorization seeks the prime factorization of a positive integer N. For N>1, this means identifying its prime factors and their multiplicities; one has the empty prime factorization. Finding one proper divisor 1<d<N is useful progress, but need not finish the job: factor d and N/d further until all factors are prime numbers.
For example, 77=7⋅11 is a semiprime, whereas 231=3⋅7⋅11 has three prime factors. Primality testing asks whether a proposed integer is prime; it need not return a factor when the answer is no. Trial division is a direct factoring method: try division by small prime numbers until a divisor is found. More elaborate methods obtain a proper divisor through a greatest common divisor of N with a specially constructed integer.
The beautiful trick in congruence of squares is that two integers with equal squares modulo N can reveal different factors through their sum and difference. In the worked N=77 example, 202≡132(mod77) gives gcd(20−13,77)=7 and gcd(20+13,77)=11. Computing those greatest common divisors uses the Euclidean algorithm; it does not require trying every potential factor. A factor base supplies a systematic way to construct useful equal-square relations. [ref].
This connection is useful in cryptography because recovering the factors of an RSA cryptosystem modulus defeats the factoring assumption behind its construction. That application concerns large, carefully chosen inputs; the small examples here explain the arithmetic mechanism and are not benchmarks or estimates of present cryptographic security.

Pollard's p-1 algorithm

Words: 77
Integer factorization OurBigBook.com
For an integer n to be factored, John Pollard's method chooses an integer a coprime to n and an exponent M divisible by many small prime powers. Compute d=gcd(aM−1,n) by modular exponentiation and the Euclidean algorithm. If 1<d<n, it is a proper factor. If a prime divisor p of n has p−1∣M, Fermat's little theorem ensures p∣d; success requires some other prime divisor not to divide aM−1. Common choices are M=B! and M=lcm(1,…,B). The method exploits a smooth p−1, rather than a small factor p itself.

General number field sieve

Words: 60
Integer factorization OurBigBook.com
A general-purpose classical integer factorization algorithm combining polynomial relations, arithmetic in number fields and sparse linear algebra to construct congruent squares modulo the input. Its familiar general-input complexity estimate is heuristic and subexponential in the input's value, roughly exp(O(n1/3(logn)2/3)) for n input bits. This is not polynomial in the bit length. Special input structure, small factors and preprocessing can make other algorithms preferable.

Ordered factorization

Words: 51
Integer factorization OurBigBook.com
An ordered factorization of a positive integer n>1 is an ordered list of factors greater than one whose product is n. For example, 6, 2⋅3, and 3⋅2 are the three ordered factorizations of 6. Taking successive partial products gives a bijection with strictly increasing divisor chains from 1 to n.

Pollard's rho algorithm

Words: 57 Articles: 1
Integer factorization OurBigBook.com
An integer factorization algorithm that iterates a simple map such as x↦x2+cmodn and searches for a nontrivial greatest common divisor of n and the difference of two iterates. A collision modulo an unknown prime factor can reveal that factor before a collision modulo n. A cycle detection schedule such as Floyd's cycle-finding algorithm limits the number of stored iterates. Unsuccessful choices of seed or map can be retried.

Factor base

Words: 410 Articles: 2
Integer factorization OurBigBook.com
A factor base is a finite set of small prime numbers over which selected auxiliary integers are completely factored. Some methods also record a sign coordinate for −1, which is not a prime number. A positive integer supported entirely on the chosen factor base gives an exponent vector; reducing that vector modulo two records which prime exponents are odd integers. The product is a square of a number precisely when every prime exponent is an even integer.
For the original toy N=77, use factor base {2,3,5} and the two relations
132≡15=3⋅5(mod77),402≡60=22⋅3⋅5(mod77).
(1)
The residues have exponent vectors (0,1,1) and (2,1,1) in the order (2,3,5). Adding the two vectors modulo two gives (0,0,0), so multiplying the residues gives 15⋅60=900=302. Consequently
(13⋅40)2≡302(mod77),X=13⋅40mod77=58,Y=30,
(2)
and gcd(X−Y,77)=7 and gcd(X+Y,77)=11. Neither individual residue was a square; combining the relations made all exponents even.
In a larger collection, choose relations xi2​≡ri​(modN) with positive residues ri​=∏j=1B​pjeji​​. If a nonempty selection I has an even sum in every exponent coordinate, set
X=∏i∈I​xi​modN,Y=∏j=1B​pj21​∑i∈I​eji​​modN.
(3)
Then X2≡Y2(modN). Finding such a selection is a linear dependence problem over the finite field F2​: the indicator vector of the chosen relations belongs to the kernel of a linear map given by the parity matrix. This is why a problem about prime factors recruits linear algebra. The final congruence of squares may still be trivial, so another selection can be needed. [ref].
There is a tradeoff: a small factor base gives a smaller parity matrix, but fewer auxiliary integers factor completely over it. A larger factor base accepts more relations but makes the linear algebra larger. Negative auxiliary values need an additional sign coordinate, and a selected product needs even sign parity as well as even prime exponents. Pomerance's account explains this balance and the historical development of combining smooth relations; the toy example omits algorithm-specific sieving and running-time claims. [ref].

Odd part of a positive integer (n=2v2​(n)d)

Words: 78
Integer factorization OurBigBook.com
The odd part of a positive integer n is the unique odd positive integer d obtained by repeatedly dividing n by two. The process terminates because the positive integers decrease. If 2rd=2se with d,e odd, then r>s would make e even and s>r would make d even; hence r=s and d=e. Two positive integers have the same odd part exactly when their ratio is an integral power of two. The odd positive integers therefore give representatives for the resulting equivalence classes.

Congruence of squares (a2≡b2(modN))

Words: 458 Articles: 1
Integer factorization OurBigBook.com
A congruence of squares says that two integers a,b have the same square modulo a positive integer N. Factoring their difference of squares gives
a2≡b2(modN)⟹N∣(a−b)(a+b).
(4)
A useful integer factorization results when gcd(a−b,N) or gcd(a+b,N) is a proper divisor of N. Divisibility of a product does not generally force divisibility of either factor by all of N: different prime factors of N can divide different parts of that product.
For N=77, 202−132=231=3⋅77. Therefore
gcd(20−13,77)=gcd(7,77)=7,gcd(20+13,77)=gcd(33,77)=11.
(5)
Thus 77=7⋅11. The prime seven divides the difference, while eleven divides the sum. These computations already give a complete prime factorization because seven and eleven are prime numbers.
The Chinese remainder theorem explains the hidden sign choices. The four congruence classes solving z2≡15(mod77) have representatives 13,20,57,64. Modulo seven each is 1 or −1; modulo eleven each is 2 or −2. Two independent sign choices produce four roots. The inputs thirteen and twenty agree modulo seven and disagree by sign modulo eleven, allowing their sum and difference to separate the two prime factors.
For distinct odd prime numbers p,q, N=pq and gcd(b,N)=1, a solution a2≡b2(modN) with a≡b and a≡−b modulo N yields both proper factors by the two greatest common divisors. For a general composite integer, a proper divisor need not itself be prime; further factoring can remain. If a≡b or a≡−b(modN) in the coprime case, the two calculations return N and one instead. A factor base helps generate relations, but does not ensure every resulting relation is useful.
For historical context, Pomerance describes Kraitchik's 1920s enhancement of the difference-of-squares approach associated with Fermat: seek a difference that is a multiple of N, rather than exactly N. His account also notes antecedents in Gauss and Seelhoff, so this is not an attribution of the whole idea to a single inventor. [ref].

Nontrivial square root of unity modulo an integer (z2≡1(modN),z≡±1(modN))

Congruence of squares OurBigBook.com
For an odd integer N>1, a nontrivial square root of unity modulo N is a residue z with z2≡1(modN) and z≡±1(modN). Then both gcd(z−1,N) and gcd(z+1,N) are proper divisors. For N=77, z=34 works: 342≡1(mod77), gcd(33,77)=11, and gcd(35,77)=7.
A congruence of squares with gcd(b,N)=1 converts to this form by z≡ab−1(modN), using a modular multiplicative inverse. In the a=20,b=13 example, 13−1≡6(mod77), so z≡20⋅6≡43(mod77). It yields gcd(42,77)=7 and gcd(44,77)=11. Nontriviality requires mixed sign choices across prime factors, which an odd prime number modulus cannot provide.

Fermat number (Fn​=22n+1)

Words: 652 Articles: 4
Number theory OurBigBook.com
A Fermat number is the positive integer Fn​=22n+1, indexed by a nonnegative integer n. The first five are 3,5,17,257,65537, all prime numbers; the next is the composite number F5​=4294967297=641⋅6700417. This family offers a compact lesson in number theory: a very persuasive finite pattern can fail, while an exact divisibility relation settles a gigantic case with little computation.
Why does the exponent itself have the form 2n? Suppose m=ab is a positive integer with an odd integer factor b>1. The polynomial factorization xb+1=(x+1)(xb−1−xb−2+⋯−x+1) shows that 2a+1 is a proper divisor of 2m+1. Consequently, if 2m+1 is a prime number, m must be a power of two. That is a necessary condition, rather than a promise that the surviving candidates are prime.
The Fermat number product identity makes distinct Fermat numbers coprime integers. Thus every term has a prime factor absent from all earlier terms, whether or not that term is itself a prime number. This gives an explicit route to infinitely many different prime numbers, without establishing that infinitely many terms of this particular sequence are prime. Meanwhile the prime divisor of a Fermat number criterion filters possible factors through a small multiplicative order calculation.
The family also links arithmetic to Euclidean geometry: a constructible regular polygon can have a number of sides equal to a power of two times a product of distinct Fermat primes. The Gauss-Wantzel theorem gives the precise criterion. For instance, 15=3⋅5 and 17 qualify, but 9=32 does not. The word "distinct" matters. Carl Pomerance describes this connection in Primality testing: then and now by Carl Pomerance (slide 18).
Historically, Leonhard Euler records Pierre de Fermat's proposed primality pattern, then refutes it by finding the factor 641 of F5​. His paper was presented in 1732 and published in 1738; those are different events, not competing dates for one publication.[ref]
A short modern check needs only two representations of 641:
641=5⋅27+1=54+24.
(6)
In modular arithmetic these give 54228≡1 and 54≡−24(mod641). Substitution yields 232≡−1(mod641), so 641∣F5​. This verifies the factor directly; it does not claim to reconstruct Euler's search process.

For each positive integer n, the product of the preceding Fermat numbers is two less than the next:
∏j=0n−1​Fj​=22n−1=Fn​−2.
(7)
For example, 3⋅5⋅17=255=257−2. The identity telescopes by repeated difference of squares: (22j−1)(22j+1)=22j+1−1. Its usefulness is that a huge integer product exposes a tiny difference, two, from the next term.

Fermat number product identity OurBigBook.com
If m<n, a common divisor of Fm​ and Fn​ divides both Fn​−2, by the Fermat number product identity, and Fn​. It therefore divides two. Both Fermat numbers are odd integers, so their greatest common divisor is one. Each term's prime factors are consequently different from the prime factors of every other term.

Fermat number OurBigBook.com
For a prime number p, the exact criterion is
p∣Fn​⟺ordp​(2)=2n+1,n≥0,
(8)
where p must be different from two and ordp​(2) is the multiplicative order of two modulo p. If p∣Fn​, then 22n≡−1(modp): the order divides 2n+1 but not 2n, so it is exactly 2n+1. Conversely, that order makes 22n a square root of unity different from one in the prime field Fp​; it must be −1, because (x−1)(x+1)=0 has no other roots in a field.
For example, modulo seventeen the powers of two are 2,4,8,16,15,13,9,1. Their first return to one occurs after eight steps. The half-way value is 16=−1(mod17), proving that 17∣F2​. Likewise, ord641​(2)=64 identifies 641 as a prime factor of F5​. These are statements about divisibility, not evidence that the entire Fermat number is prime.
The multiplicative order always divides p−1, by Fermat's little theorem, so p≡1(mod2n+1). In particular, for n≥1 every prime divisor of a Fermat number is one modulo four. That weaker modular congruence is insufficient: thirteen is one modulo four, but ord13​(2)=12, which is not a power of two. It divides no Fermat number at any index. The exact order criterion explains the whole family, instead of testing finitely many terms.

The restriction matters: F1​=5 has factor five, which is not one modulo eight.

Normal number (limN→∞​FN​(w)=K−r)

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Number theory OurBigBook.com
A real number is normal in an integer base K≥2 when every finite word of digits occurs in its positional notation with the same limiting digit block frequency as every other word of the same length. Write its fractional part as x=0.d1​d2​… in base K, using the expansion that is not eventually all K−1 digits when two expansions are possible. For every length r≥1 and every word w∈{0,…,K−1}r, the requirement is
limN→∞​N−r+1∣{1≤j≤N−r+1:(dj​,…,dj+r−1​)=w}∣​=K−r.
(9)
Occurrences overlap: the word 11 occurs twice in 111. There are Kr possible words of length r, so K−r is the equal share for each. In a decimal representation, this means frequency 1/10 for each digit, 1/100 for each pair, and 1/1000 for each triple, continuing through every finite length. The definition agrees with that used by Copeland and Erdős in their work on explicit normal numbers. [ref]
The appeal is that a precise, deterministic real number can have the same limiting digit block frequencies as repeated draws from a uniform distribution on a finite set, with independence between draws. Champernowne constant is an explicit example. Normality is useful for studying digit distribution, but balanced digits alone establish only a simply normal number, and a finite sample cannot establish any of these infinite limits.
Émile Borel introduced normal numbers and established their prevalence in his 1909 paper applying probability to number theory; the stronger all-base statement is discussed under absolutely normal number. [ref]

Digit block frequency (FN​(w))

Words: 123
Normal number OurBigBook.com
For a finite prefix of N≥r digits in positional notation, the digit block frequency FN​(w) of a length-r word w is its number of overlapping occurrences divided by N−r+1, the number of available starting positions. All such digit block frequencies sum to one. The infinite limit used for a normal number can instead divide counts by N: the factor (N−r+1)/N tends to one for fixed r.
For the six binary digits 010101, the single-digit counts are three zeros and three ones. Its five adjacent pairs are 01,10,01,10,01, giving
F6​(00)=F6​(11)=0,F6​(01)=53​,F6​(10)=52​.
(10)
This example explains both the overlapping convention and the end correction in a finite sample. The corresponding infinite binary expansion has pair frequencies 0,1/2,1/2,0, rather than the four values 1/4 required of a normal number in base two.

Simply normal number (limN→∞​FN​(a)=1/K)

Words: 158
Normal number OurBigBook.com
A real number is simply normal in base K if each individual digit in its positional notation has limiting digit block frequency 1/K. This is the length-one part of the definition of a normal number. It places no equal-frequency requirement on longer words.
For example, x=0.010101…2​=1/3 is a simply normal number in base two: each binary digit has frequency 1/2. But 00 and 11 never occur, and 01 and 10 each have frequency 1/2. Thus x is not a normal number in base two. Even a sequence that looks more complicated, such as the deterministic Thue–Morse sequence, must be tested against the actual digit block frequency definition; visual complexity is no substitute for it.
The decimal representation y=0.01234567890123456789… makes the same point in base ten. Every digit has frequency 1/10, yet the only adjacent pairs are
01,12,23,34,45,56,67,78,89,90.
(11)
Each has limiting digit block frequency 1/10; the other ninety pairs have frequency zero. A normal number in base ten requires 1/100 for every one of the hundred pairs. This rational number is a simply normal number in base ten, but it is not a normal number in that base.

Champernowne constant (C10​=0.123456789101112…)

Words: 300
Normal number OurBigBook.com
Form Champernowne constant by using concatenation to join the decimal representations of the positive integers 1,2,3,… after the decimal point. Champernowne proved in 1933 that this particular real number is a normal number in base ten. The construction is striking because its rule is completely explicit, while all finite words have the prescribed limiting digit block frequencies. [ref] Copeland and Erdős explicitly recall this result at the start of their own paper. [ref]
The first 100000 digits of Champernowne constant have the following exact counts, in digit order 0,1,…,9:
(8642,19753,11111,8642,8642,8642,8642,8642,8642,8642).
(12)
For the 99999 adjacent pairs fully inside that prefix, the words 00,01,12,99 occur 642,1753,2088,753 times respectively. Thus, for example, F100000​(12)=2088/99999, which is about 0.02088, rather than 0.01. The prefix ends partway through the decimal representation of 22222; the many leading ones in earlier positive integers help explain the visible imbalance.
These are finite counts, not a proof of the normal number theorem: a finite prefix can be followed by an all-zero tail. The theorem for Champernowne constant concerns the infinite limit, and establishes base-ten normality, rather than absolute normality. Nor do computations prove normality for familiar constants: the normality of Pi and Euler's number remains unproved, as discussed by Bailey and Borwein. [ref]

Normality and equidistribution under integer multiplication (x normal in base K⟺({Knx})n≥0​ equidistributed)

Normal number OurBigBook.com
A real number x is a normal number in base K exactly when its iterates under the integer multiplication map on the circle, TK​(x)={Kx}, form an equidistributed sequence. Braces denote the fractional part. Multiplication by K shifts the positional notation one digit to the left:
TKn​(x)={Knx}=0.dn+1​dn+2​…in base K.
(13)
A length-r word with base-K integer value a specifies the half-open interval [a/Kr,(a+1)/Kr), whose length is K−r. Visiting that interval is exactly encountering that word at the next digit position. These digit intervals form arbitrarily fine grids, so their correct limiting visiting frequencies imply equidistribution on every interval. This converts a question about digits into one about a dynamical system. Bailey and Crandall develop this connection using equidistribution of the fractional parts of Knx. [ref]
In base ten the word 12 corresponds to [0.12,0.13). For Champernowne constant, counting the visits T10n​(x) for 0≤n≤99998 gives precisely the 2088 occurrences of 12 in its first 100000 digits. For x=1/3, the base-two integer multiplication map on the circle instead alternates between 1/3 and 2/3; it never visits [0,1/4), the interval for 00. This two-point orbit is not an equidistributed sequence.

Absolutely normal number

Words: 168
Normal number OurBigBook.com
An absolutely normal number is a normal number in every integer base K≥2. This requires every finite word in every such positional notation to have its appropriate limiting digit block frequency. Knowing base-ten normality alone does not establish absolute normality; the base is part of the statement.
Borel's 1909 result says that absolute normality holds almost everywhere for Lebesgue measure: within [0,1) the exceptions form a Lebesgue null set. In particular, the set of absolutely normal numbers has Lebesgue measure one there. This is a statement about the size of an exceptional set, not a test for a specified constant. [ref] [ref]
A modern route uses the Birkhoff ergodic theorem and ergodicity of integer multiplication on the circle. For each fixed base and digit interval, the time proportion equals its Lebesgue measure almost everywhere. The bases and finite words form countable sets, so a countable intersection of these measure-one sets still has Lebesgue measure one. For an absolutely normal number, the word 11 therefore has frequency 1/4 in base two, 1/9 in base three, and 1/100 in base ten. The same symbols represent different intervals in different bases.

Natural density (d(S))

Words: 645 Articles: 3
Number theory OurBigBook.com
For a set S of nonnegative integers, its natural density is the limiting proportion of the first N nonnegative integers that belong to S:
d(S)=limN→∞​N∣S∩{0,…,N−1}∣​,
(14)
provided this limit exists. Write CS​(N)=∣S∩{0,…,N−1}∣ for the counting function. The numerator is a finite cardinality; the denominator is exactly N, including zero. Every existing natural density lies between zero and one.
For the even nonnegative integers E={0,2,4,…}, there are m elements below N=2m and m+1 below N=2m+1. Thus CE​(N)=⌈N/2⌉ using the ceiling function, and d(E)=1/2. For the square numbers Q={0,1,4,9,…}, the exact count for N≥1 is
CQ​(N)=⌊N−1​⌋+1,d(Q)=0.
(15)
The floor function counts the allowed indices 1,…,⌊N−1​⌋, and the extra one counts zero. At N=10, the square numbers below ten are 0,1,4,9, so the proportion is 4/10; at N=100, it is 10/100. The count grows like the square root of N, while the denominator grows like N.
The prime numbers also have natural density zero. If P is their set, the Prime number theorem gives CP​(N)∼N/logN, hence CP​(N)/N→0. The Prime number theorem is a substantial result about the count, rather than a consequence of the fact that there are infinitely many prime numbers. [ref]
Why use natural density when cardinality already measures size? The even nonnegative integers, the square numbers, and the prime numbers all have the same countably infinite cardinality, yet their proportions among large initial integer intervals differ. Natural density distinguishes frequent membership from sparse membership. Equivalently, under a uniform distribution on a finite set of N possible nonnegative integers, CS​(N)/N is the probability of landing in S. A set without natural density shows why this limiting proportion need not exist.

Include the positive integers in [1,2),[4,8),[16,32),[64,128),…, and exclude the intervening integer intervals and zero. Equivalently, include [22k,22k+1)∩Z for k≥0. Each included block is large enough to raise the running proportion; the following excluded block lowers it again.
With CA​(N)=∣A∩{0,…,N−1}∣, the exact boundary counts follow from a geometric series:
CA​(4k)=∑j=0k−1​4j=34k−1​,CA​(2⋅4k)=∑j=0k​4j=34k+1−1​.
(16)
The first sum is empty at k=0. Dividing by the corresponding boundary, rather than using one denominator for both, gives

For example, CA​(16)=1+4=5, whereas CA​(32)=1+4+16=21, yielding proportions 5/16 and 21/32. For 4k≤N≤2⋅4k, the exact count is (4k−1)/3+N−4k; for 2⋅4k≤N≤4k+1 it stays (4k+1−1)/3. Hence the proportion increases through each included block and decreases through each excluded block. These boundary subsequences give the actual limit inferior and limit superior:
liminfN→∞​NCA​(N)​=31​,limsupN→∞​NCA​(N)​=32​.

Words: 180
Natural density OurBigBook.com
For a subset A of the positive integers, its upper asymptotic density is
d(A)=limsupN→∞​N∣A∩{1,…,N}∣​.

The limit superior keeps the largest limiting proportion even when the running proportions oscillate. Because they lie in [0,1], this limit superior always exists in [0,1]. If natural density exists, upper asymptotic density equals it.
The convention here uses 1,…,N, while natural density above uses 0,…,N−1. Replacing one interval by the other changes a count by at most one, so the proportions differ by at most 1/N and have the same limit superior. For the set without natural density above, the count in {1,…,16} is six rather than five, because 16 is included and zero is absent. Nevertheless its upper asymptotic density is exactly 2/3. The even positive integers have upper asymptotic density 1/2 and the prime numbers have upper asymptotic density zero.
The useful feature is that a large proportion along arbitrarily large initial integer intervals already supplies structure. The Szemerédi theorem says that positive upper asymptotic density forces arithmetic progressions of every finite length, with positive common difference, even without an existing natural density. Szemerédi's 1975 paper resolved this general finite-length problem; it makes density a bridge from counting to additive structure. [ref]

Lagrange's four-square theorem (n=a2+b2+c2+d2)

Words: 661
Number theory OurBigBook.com
Every nonnegative integer is a sum of squares with four terms, with zero terms allowed. Precisely, for every integer n≥0, there exist nonnegative integers a,b,c,d such that

(20)
Allowing arbitrary integer roots gives the same statement: changing a root to its absolute value leaves the resulting square number unchanged. Four is a uniform upper bound on the number of nonzero terms, rather than a demand for four positive terms. Repeated square numbers are allowed. Conrad states the positive case and explicitly explains the role of zero terms; n=0 follows by taking all four roots zero. [ref]
The small cases make the convention visible:
01237​=02+02+02+02,=12+02+02+02,=12+12+02+02,=12+12+12+02,=22+12+12+12.​
(21)
In particular, 1 could not be a sum of squares with four strictly positive roots, since each term would be at least one. Geometrically, a square of integer side length a has area a2: the theorem says that any nonnegative whole-number total area can be split into at most four such square areas. It does not assert that those squares tile one larger square or a prescribed rectangle.
Why does the fourth term matter? Two square numbers do not suffice for 3: in modular arithmetic, a square number has remainder zero or one modulo four, so their sum cannot be three modulo four. The sum of two squares theorem gives a complete criterion for the positive integers representable with two terms. Even three terms leave gaps. A square number has remainder 0,1, or 4 modulo eight; adding three of these, with repetition allowed, never gives seven modulo eight. Thus 7,15,23,31,… cannot be sums of three square numbers, although Lagrange's four-square theorem represents all of them with four. This also proves that the bound four cannot be reduced to three.
The modulo-eight obstruction is not the only way that three terms can fail. For example, 28 needs four: if three square numbers added to 28, their remainders modulo four would force all three roots even. Dividing by four would then express 7 as a sum of three square numbers, contradicting the preceding calculation. These short checks explain the examples without requiring a full classification of sums of three square numbers.
The practical benefit of Lagrange's four-square theorem is an existence guarantee for a family of Diophantine equations: for every nonnegative integer n, the displayed equation has an integer solution. It does not specify a unique solution. For instance, 65=82+12+02+02=72+42+02+02=62+42+32+22. To find a representation by a finite search, enumerate 0≤d≤c≤b≤a≤⌊n​⌋ and test the sum. The floor function supplies a finite bound because no single term can exceed n, and sorting roots removes duplicate orderings without discarding any possible sum. The theorem guarantees that the search succeeds.
A greedy algorithm that repeatedly subtracts the largest available square number need not find four terms: for 23 it chooses 16+4+1+1+1, while 23=9+9+4+1 uses four. The appeal of the theorem is this gap between local choices and a global promise: individual square numbers become farther apart, and two or three terms leave arithmetic obstructions, yet four terms cover every nonnegative integer.
For historical orientation, Conrad dates Lagrange's four-square theorem to 1770 and identifies the memoir as Démonstration d'un théorème d'arithmétique: it appeared in the Berlin Academy's volume for the year 1770, published in 1772, pages 123–133. Keeping the volume year and publication year distinct avoids an apparent conflict between dates. [ref]

Exponentiation by squaring (an)

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Number theory OurBigBook.com
Exponentiation by squaring computes an integer power by reading the exponent's binary expansion. Appending a binary digit b to a prefix of value p replaces p by 2p+b, so the corresponding power changes by
a2p+b=(ap)2ab,b∈{0,1}.
(22)
Each new digit requires one squaring and, only for digit one, one further multiplication. The number of digits grows with the logarithm of the exponent, making this useful for modular exponentiation, primality testing, and powers of matrices using matrix multiplication.[ref]
For a concrete calculation, 13=(1101)2​=8+4+1, so 313=38⋅34⋅3. The optimized left-to-right algorithm used here instead keeps one accumulated power: initialize r=3 from the leading digit one, then process only the remaining digits 1,0,1:
1111101101​:r=3,:r=32⋅3=27,:r=272=729,:r=7292⋅3=531441⋅3=1594323.​
(23)
Thus 313=1594323, using three squarings and two further multiplications, instead of twelve successive multiplications starting at 3.
For a general positive integer n=(bℓ−1​⋯b0​)2​ with leading digit bℓ−1​=1, set r=a and, for i=ℓ−2,…,0, first replace r by r2, then multiply it by a if bi​=1. Return r. This explicitly skips the leading digit's otherwise unnecessary operations on one. A Computational Introduction to Number Theory and Algebra by Victor Shoup (Section 3.4, pp. 65–66) presents the version initialized at one and processing every digit; the optimization here makes the counting convention unambiguous.
The loop invariant is r=ap, where p is the value of the digits already read. Initially p=1 and r=a. If the next digit is b, then squaring and optionally multiplying give r′=a2p+b, exactly the next prefix. At termination p=n. This proof uses associativity of multiplication; it works in any monoid, including matrices with the identity matrix as identity element, and needs no commutativity between different bases.
For n=0, return the identity element without performing a multiplication. This is the empty-product convention a0=1; if a=0, the algorithm therefore returns one for 00 by convention, rather than resolving its meaning in every mathematical setting. Negative integer exponents require an inverse element: compute (a−1)−n, counting the inversion separately. Over the integers, such an inverse generally leaves the integers, and a zero base has no inverse.

Coupled binary exponentiation (pxk=An,qyl=Bm)

Words: 108
Exponentiation by squaring OurBigBook.com
To compute two nonnegative integer powers in one while loop, maintain a separate accumulator, current base and remaining exponent for each exponentiation by squaring. The paired loop invariant is pxk=An and qyl=Bm. For each positive remaining exponent, transfer its odd factor to its accumulator and halve the exponent while squaring its base. A zero remaining exponent is left unchanged. The mathematical integer k+l is a loop variant: at least one positive term strictly decreases in every iteration. Both powers are therefore complete when the loop stops. The iteration count is O(log(max(n,m)+1)), with constant space and a constant number of multiplications per iteration. This is an exact-arithmetic identity; floating-point rounding introduces a separate error in a numerical implementation.

Simultaneous exponentiation by squaring (pj​ujk​=ajn​)

Words: 88
Exponentiation by squaring OurBigBook.com
Several powers with one nonnegative exponent can share a single exponent-halving loop. For bases aj​, maintain accumulators pj​, current bases uj​ and a remaining exponent k, with loop invariants pj​ujk​=ajn​. For an odd k, multiply every accumulator by its current base; square every current base and halve k. The equalities are preserved in parallel, and the nonnegative loop variant k strictly decreases. For a fixed number of bases this uses O(log(n+1)) arithmetic operations and one loop, while keeping each base in the intended numeric type.

Binary powering multiplication count (C(n)=ℓ+wt(n)−2)

Words: 270
Exponentiation by squaring OurBigBook.com
For the optimized left-to-right exponentiation by squaring algorithm, let ℓ=⌊log2​n⌋+1 be the length of the binary expansion of a positive integer n, and let w=wt(n) be its Hamming weight, the number of digits equal to one. There are exactly ℓ−1 digits after the leading one, and exactly w−1 remaining ones. Therefore the count is
S(n)=ℓ−1,T(n)=w−1,C(n)=S(n)+T(n)=ℓ+w−2.
(24)
Here S counts squarings and T counts further multiplications by the base; every squaring counts as one multiplication in C. Assignment, digit reading, and any inversion are outside this count. The formula includes n=1, which requires zero multiplications; define C(0)=0 separately.
For a fixed length ℓ, the bounds are ℓ−1≤C(n)≤2ℓ−2. A power of two reaches the lower bound because its Hamming weight is one; n=2ℓ−1 reaches the upper bound because all digits are one. For n=13, ℓ=4 and w=3, giving C(13)=5. Thus the arithmetic operation count is O(log(n+1)) in Big O notation, but inputs of similar magnitude can have different counts.
This is a count for the specified algorithm, not a claim that it always minimizes multiplications among all methods. For instance, at n=15 the count is six, but the powers with exponents 1,2,3,6,12,15 can be built in five multiplications: square, multiply by a, square, square, then multiply by the already stored a3. Saving operations this way uses a different schedule and stored intermediate powers.

Modular exponentiation (abmodm)

Words: 596 Articles: 1
Exponentiation by squaring OurBigBook.com
Modular exponentiation computes the remainder anmodm for an integer base a, a nonnegative integer exponent n, and, here, an integer modulus m≥2. It applies exponentiation by squaring while reducing after each multiplication, including each squaring. The result is the unique representative in {0,…,m−1}. There is no requirement that the base be coprime to the modulus when the exponent is nonnegative.[ref]
Take a=2, n=13=(1101)2​, and m=17. Initialize r=2; the remaining digits give
111101101​:22mod17=4,4⋅2mod17=8,:82mod17=64mod17=13,:132mod17=169mod17=16,16⋅2mod17=15.​
(25)
Hence 213mod17=15. The final operation multiplies 16 by 2, since the preceding square has already been reduced. The computation never needs to construct 213=8192.
In general reduce the base first, x=amodm. For n>0, initialize r=x and process the remaining binary digits with r←r2modm, followed, for a digit one, by r←rxmodm. The loop invariant is
0≤r<m,r≡ap(modm),
(26)
where p is the processed prefix value. The congruence is preserved because modular arithmetic respects multiplication: if u≡v(modm), then u2≡v2 and ux≡va(modm). Thus changing representatives never changes the final congruence class.
Both factors in every product are less than m, so the unreduced product is less than m2, and the stored result is again less than m. The same bounds hold for a gigantic exponent, such as n=21000: there are 1000 squarings, each on bounded-size residues. For base two, the corresponding ordinary power would have 21000+1 binary digits. The benefit is avoiding the huge ordinary power altogether, rather than constructing it and taking one final remainder. Initial reduction is essential when the supplied base is much larger than the modulus.
For n=0, return 1 under the same empty-product convention as exponentiation by squaring. For n=−k<0, require gcd(a,m)=1, find the modular multiplicative inverse a−1modm, and compute (a−1)kmodm; the extended Euclidean algorithm can find that inverse. Its cost is separate from the positive-exponent binary powering multiplication count. For example, 2−1≡9(mod17), while 2−1mod4 is undefined because 2 and 4 are not coprime.
A reversible computation gives the coherent quantum modular exponentiation used in quantum order finding and discrete-logarithm Fourier sampling.

Bit cost of modular exponentiation (O(ℓL2))

Words: 248
Modular exponentiation OurBigBook.com
The binary powering multiplication count counts arithmetic operations. The time complexity measured in operations on individual bits also depends on operand lengths. Put L=⌊log2​m⌋+1, the binary length of the modulus, and let ℓ be the positive exponent's binary length. Stored residues use at most L bits, and an unreduced product uses at most 2L bits.
With ordinary long multiplication and division with remainder, one modular product costs O(L2) operations on bits. Combining that cost with O(ℓ) modular products gives
bit cost of the powering loop=O(ℓL2).
(27)
This bound includes reductions in the loop, and assumes the base has already been reduced and the exponent is available as a binary expansion. Reading the exponent takes O(ℓ) additional work; initial reduction of a very long base depends on its input length, and an inverse for a negative exponent adds further work. More generally, if a modular product costs R(L) operations on bits, the powering loop costs O(ℓR(L)). Faster multiplication and reduction methods can improve the quadratic bound.[ref]
For ordinary integer powers with ∣a∣≥2, the output itself has ⌊nlog2​∣a∣⌋+1 binary digits. Even writing it takes work proportional to that length. Consequently O(log(n+1)) multiplications does not imply O(log(n+1)) operations on bits: the operands grow during ordinary exponentiation by squaring, whereas modular exponentiation keeps them bounded by the modulus. A squaring or multiplication by a small fixed base can also cost less than a general product, so equal counts need not mean equal running times.

Composite number

Words: 122 Articles: 1
Number theory OurBigBook.com
A composite number is an integer greater than one that is not a prime number. Equivalently, it has a factorization n=ab with integers a,b>1. Thus 4=2⋅2, 9=3⋅3, and 12=3⋅4 are composite numbers; one is neither a composite number nor a prime number.
Every composite number has a prime factor at most its square root. In 91=7⋅13, seven is the smaller factor and lies below 91​; in 49=72, equality occurs. This square-root bound makes trial division finite and lets the sieve of Eratosthenes stop marking with prime numbers beyond N​ when listing prime numbers up to N.

Semiprime (N=pq)

Words: 41
Composite number OurBigBook.com
A semiprime is a composite number that is a product of exactly two prime numbers, counted with multiplicity. For example, 6=2⋅3 and 9=32 are semiprimes. Distinct factors give φ(pq)=(p−1)(q−1) for the Euler totient function, whereas equal factors give φ(p2)=p(p−1). This distinction matters when constructing a uniform coprime state for a semiprime.

Euler's theorem (aφ(n)≡1(modn))

Words: 753 Articles: 3
Number theory OurBigBook.com
For an integer modulus n≥2 and an integer a with greatest common divisor gcd(a,n)=1, Euler's theorem, also called the Fermat-Euler theorem, states
aφ(n)≡1(modn).
(28)
Here Euler's totient function φ(n) counts the units in the unit group U(n)=(Z/nZ)×. These congruence classes have modular multiplicative inverses, equivalently their representatives are coprime to n. The guaranteed return to one permits exponent reduction for units.[ref]
For a prime number p, φ(p)=p−1, recovering Fermat's little theorem in the form ap−1≡1(modp) when p∤a. Multiplying by a and separately handling p∣a gives ap≡a(modp) for every integer a. For a composite number used as the integer modulus, a nonzero congruence class can be a nonunit.
Modulo twelve, the units have representatives 1,5,7,11, so Euler's totient function gives φ(12)=4. Multiplication by five produces
1⟼5⟼1,7⟼11⟼7(mod12).
(29)
Thus this permutation has two permutation cycles, each of length two. In particular 52≡1(mod12), and the guaranteed return 54≡1 follows. The number of units need not be the length of one permutation cycle. Modulo fifteen, multiplication by seven similarly gives the two permutation cycles (1,7,4,13) and (2,14,8,11), covering all eight units. The powers of seven follow the permutation cycle containing one; the other permutation cycle shows that these powers do not visit every unit.
There is a stronger obstruction for a nonunit than just an occasional failed calculation. If a positive integer d>1 divides both a and n, then ak≡0(modd) for every k≥1, so ak cannot be congruent to one modulo n. For example, gcd(3,15)=3 and 3φ(15)=38≡6(mod15), rather than one. Such a base has no multiplicative order modulo that integer modulus.[ref]

Multiplication by a unit permutes reduced residues (u↦auon U(n))

Euler's theorem OurBigBook.com
Choose a reduced residue system u1​,…,uφ(n)​. For a unit modulo n a, the bijection u↦au on the unit group has inverse u↦a−1u. Comparing products before and after this permutation gives
P=∏i=1φ(n)​ui​≡∏i=1φ(n)​(aui​)=aφ(n)P(modn).
(30)
The product P is a unit; its modular inverse cancels it, proving Euler's theorem. Merely being nonzero would not justify cancellation.[ref]
In the modulo-twelve example, P=1⋅5⋅7⋅11=385≡1(mod12). The permuted representatives 5,1,11,7 have the same product, while the unreduced products (5⋅1)(5⋅5)(5⋅7)(5⋅11) equal 54P. Equating these products modulo twelve exposes the fourth power without calculating it directly. Using all nonzero congruence classes instead would include nonunits, whose product need not permit cancellation.

Exponent reduction for units (ak≡akmodφ(n)(modn))

Euler's theorem OurBigBook.com
For a unit modulo n a and a nonnegative integer k, division with remainder writes k=qφ(n)+r with 0≤r<φ(n). Euler's theorem then gives
ak=(aφ(n))qar≡ar(modn).

This replaces a potentially enormous exponent by a small remainder. The exponent itself is reduced modulo Euler's totient function, while the powers are reduced modulo n: these are different integer moduli.
For a worked modulo-fifteen calculation, seven is coprime to fifteen and φ(15)=8. Therefore
2029=253⋅8+5,72029≡75(mod15).

Use exponentiation by squaring on the remaining exponent 5=(101)2​, reducing after each multiplication:
72≡49≡4,74≡42≡1,75≡1⋅7≡7(mod15).

Thus 72029mod15=7. Modular exponentiation supplies the computation; Euler's theorem supplies the optional shortening of its exponent. Exponentiation by squaring also works for nonunit bases, without using this shortening.
The guaranteed exponent φ(n) is a common return exponent and an upper bound on the shortest period; it need not be that period. The multiplicative order d=ordn​(a) is the least positive return exponent for the chosen unit. The Carmichael function λ(n) is the least positive return exponent that works for every unit. Their precise relation is
ordn​(a)∣λ(n)∣φ(n).

Either smaller return exponent can replace φ(n) in exponent reduction for units. Modulo fifteen, ord15​(7)=λ(15)=4<8=φ(15), so 2029=507⋅4+1 gives 72029≡7 immediately. For base four the multiplicative order is only two, smaller even than λ(15). A return at exponent eight alone does not prove that the multiplicative order is eight.[ref]
If the reduced exponent is zero, the rule gives ak≡a0=1, and still requires a unit. Applying it to the nonunit three would falsely predict 38≡30=1(mod15); the actual residue is six. If one Euler witness b0​ exists modulo N, multiplication by b0​ injects the set of nonwitnesses into the set of witnesses. Indeed, the product of b0​ with a nonwitness cannot be another nonwitness, because cancellation and multiplicativity of the Jacobi symbol would make b0​ a nonwitness. Existence of an Euler witness for every odd composite integer

Euler witness OurBigBook.com
Every odd composite integer has an Euler witness. For a nonsquarefree integer, a base congruent to 1+p modulo a repeated prime factor p2 fails the Euler congruence by the binomial theorem. For a squarefree integer, use the Chinese remainder theorem to choose a base that is a quadratic nonresidue modulo one prime factor and 1 modulo another. Its Jacobi symbol is −1, while its power is 1 modulo the second factor.

Euler witness OurBigBook.com
The Solovay-Strassen primality test samples unit bases and rejects an odd candidate as composite when it finds an Euler witness. Every prime passes every base by Euler's criterion, while an odd composite passes a random base with probability at most one half.

P-adic valuation (vp​)

Words: 2k Articles: 15
Number theory OurBigBook.com
For a prime number p and a nonzero integer N, the P-adic valuation counts the exponent of p in its prime factorization:
vp​(N)=max{a∈Z≥0​:pa∣N}.
(40)
For 72=23⋅32, it gives v2​(72)=3, v3​(72)=2, and v5​(72)=0. The sign of a nonzero integer does not change these prime exponents. Relative to an ordered factor base, the valuations supply the coordinates of its exponent vector.
The P-adic valuation extends to nonzero rational numbers by vp​(a/b)=vp​(a)−vp​(b). For example, v5​(72/25)=−2 records a factor in the denominator instead of the numerator. Multiplication adds valuations, vp​(xy)=vp​(x)+vp​(y); this is the arithmetic reason why adding exponent vectors can make a product a square. In particular, a positive integer is a square of a number precisely when all its prime exponents are even integers, the criterion used by a factor base.

The p-adic integers retain arithmetic information modulo arbitrarily high powers of one prime number p. They form the subring
Zp​={x∈Qp​:∣x∣p​≤1}​
(41)
of the P-adic numbers. Their p-adic absolute value bounds the allowed denominators: 1/3 belongs to Z2​, while 1/2 does not. The name therefore describes a local arithmetic ring, not just the ordinary integers.[ref]
A concrete description gives an element by a compatible sequence of congruence classes:
Zp​=lim​n≥1​Z/pnZ,rn+1​≡rn​(modpn).
(42)
The inverse limit condition says that gaining more precision must preserve the digits already determined. Each rn​ is a residue modulo pn; choosing its least nonnegative integer representative gives 0≤rn​<pn. The ordinary integer 13 gives residues 1,1,5,13 modulo 2,4,8,16.
The useful feature is that one exact object organizes an unlimited family of finite modular arithmetic calculations. Addition and multiplication are performed modulo each pn, and the results remain compatible. A p-adic digit expansion makes this concrete:
x=∑j≥0​bj​pj,bj​∈{0,1,…,p−1},rn​=∑j=0n−1​bj​pj.
(43)
The expansion is unique and converges in the p-adic metric; its higher powers have smaller p-adic absolute value. The digit agreement and p-adic distance criterion tells exactly which finite digits a precision bound preserves.[ref]

Words: 120
p-adic integer OurBigBook.com
The p-adic integers form a complete metric space and a discrete valuation ring. Every nonzero x is uniquely pku with k=vp​(x)≥0 and u a p-adic unit. The prime p is a uniformizer, and reduction modulo p gives the residue field Fp​. The element p has no inverse inside Zp​, so the ring is not a field.
For a short ideal-classification outline, take a nonzero ideal and choose an element of smallest P-adic valuation k, which exists by the well-ordering principle. Its unit factor is invertible, so the ideal contains pk. Every other element is divisible by pk, proving that the ideal is pkZp​. Completeness follows because Zp​ is a closed subset of the complete metric space Qp​. The zero ideal is separate from this nonzero-ideal classification.

Conversely, if the index is m, the finite quotient is annihilated by m, giving mZp​⊂H. Multiplication by the unit part of m is bijective, so mZp​=pvp​(m)Zp​ is open. This proof applies to abstract subgroups without assuming beforehand that they are closed.

Legendre's formula (vp​(n!)=∑j≥1​⌊n/pj⌋)

Words: 299
P-adic valuation OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative integer n and a prime number p, the Legendre formula computes the prime exponent in a factorial without forming that huge product:
vp​(n!)=∑j≥1​⌊pjn​⌋.
(48)
Here ⌊x⌋ is the floor function. The sum is finite: every term with pj>n is zero. When n=0, all terms vanish, agreeing with 0!=1 and vp​(1)=0. The prime number hypothesis matters: a composite number does not give the same P-adic valuation or additive prime exponent. For example, the floor sum with n=6,p=4 is one, whereas 42 divides 6!=720.
Why count multiples repeatedly? Each multiple of p in 1,…,n contributes one factor of p; each multiple of p2 contributes another; and so on. A factor m with P-adic valuation a occurs in exactly the first a counts. Adding those contributions proves the formula.[ref]
For the original example n=50,p=3,
v3​(50!)=⌊350​⌋+⌊950​⌋+⌊2750​⌋=16+5+1=22.
(49)
The five multiples 9,18,27,36,45 each contribute a second factor of three. The factor 27 contributes a third, so it appears in all three rows. Equivalently, among 1,…,50 there are eleven factors of P-adic valuation one, four of valuation two, and one of valuation three: 11+2⋅4+3⋅1=22. Thus 322 divides 50!, while 323 does not.
Repeated Euclidean division provides a practical evaluation: replace q by ⌊q/p⌋, starting from q=n, and add each new quotient until it is zero. This uses only the successive quotients 16,5,1,0 for the example. The same calculation handles divisibility of binomial coefficients, where the P-adic valuations of the denominator factorials are subtracted.

For nonnegative integers x,y and an integer base p≥2,

In column addition, every arithmetic carry replaces p units in one numeral digit by one unit in the next position and therefore decreases the base-p digit sum by p−1. For prime number bases, Kummer's theorem turns this digit-sum deficit into a prime exponent.

Quadratic reciprocity compares two questions: is the prime number p a quadratic residue modulo q, and is q a quadratic residue modulo p? Let p,q be distinct odd primes. In terms of the Legendre symbol,

The two Legendre symbols have opposite signs exactly when both primes are 3 modulo 4; otherwise they are equal. Their values are nonzero because the primes are distinct. Equal signs can mean two quadratic residues or two quadratic nonresidues: reciprocity compares the answers rather than declaring either answer positive.[ref]
For a direct computation, the nonzero quadratic residues modulo 3,5,7 are respectively {1}, {1,4}, and {1,2,4}. Squaring just 1,…,(p−1)/2 suffices because x and p−x have the same square modulo an odd prime p.

Carmichael number (aN−1≡1(modN))

Words: 835 Articles: 3
Number theory OurBigBook.com
A Carmichael number is a composite number N>1 for which
aN−1≡1(modN)whenever gcd(a,N)=1.
(76)
Every unit modulo N satisfies the same modular congruence supplied by Fermat's little theorem for a prime number. The name refers to Robert Daniel Carmichael. The coprime qualification is essential: a nonunit can expose a prime factor through a greatest common divisor calculation. A Carmichael number is therefore a Fermat pseudoprime to every coprime base, rather than to every nonzero residue class.[ref]
For example,
561=3⋅11⋅17 is a Carmichael number.​
(77)
The factors are distinct prime numbers. Their predecessor numbers 2,10,16 all divide 560, so Korselt criterion applies. More explicitly, for any integer a coprime to 561, Fermat's little theorem gives
a560≡1(mod3),a560≡1(mod11),a560≡1(mod17).
(78)
The Chinese remainder theorem combines these into a560≡1(mod561). This proves all coprime bases pass from three short divisibility checks, rather than from a long table of sampled bases.
Equivalently, a composite N is a Carmichael number exactly when aN≡a(modN) for every integer a, including nonunits. The equivalence follows from Korselt criterion: modulo each prime factor, either a is zero or its nonzero power returns to one, and squarefreeness combines those congruences. This does not say a nonunit satisfies aN−1≡1. For instance a=3 gives 3560≡375(mod561), while 3561≡3(mod561); the greatest common divisor already supplies the factor three.[ref]
The Carmichael function supplies another compact description: a composite N is Carmichael exactly when λ(N)∣N−1. For 561, λ(561)=lcm(2,10,16)=80 and 560=7⋅80. In contrast, Euler's totient function gives φ(561)=320, which does not divide 560. The least common return exponent, rather than the number of units, controls this test.
The obstruction is useful to know when interpreting a Fermat primality test: even checking every coprime base cannot certify primality. The passing-base fraction for the Fermat test makes this failure quantitative. Stronger primality tests require additional structure, such as the squaring conditions in a Miller-Rabin primality test.
The historical record predates the name. Václav Šimerka's 1885 paper lists 561,1105,1729,2465,2821,6601,8911 on printed page 224, together with factorizations. This is an early published list of examples, independently of their later name.[ref]

The composite condition must be retained. A prime number is squarefree and satisfies the divisibility condition, but is excluded from the definition of a Carmichael number. Proof of Korselt criterion

Words: 147
Korselt criterion OurBigBook.com
For sufficiency, let N be composite and squarefree, with p−1∣N−1 for every prime factor p. For any integer a coprime to N, Fermat's little theorem gives aN−1≡1(modp) for every such p. Their product is N, so the Chinese remainder theorem gives the required congruence modulo N.
For necessity, first rule out a repeated factor. If N=pkm with k≥2 and gcd(p,m)=1, the Chinese remainder theorem supplies a≡1+p(modpk) and a≡1(modm). This a is coprime to N. But the binomial theorem gives
aN−1≡(1+p)N−1≡1+(N−1)p≡1−p≡1(modp2),
(80)
contradicting the Carmichael number condition. Hence N is squarefree.
Now choose a primitive root g modulo a prime factor p. Lift it to a unit modulo N by prescribing a≡g(modp) and a≡1(modN/p). The Chinese remainder theorem applies because N is squarefree. The Carmichael congruence implies gN−1≡1(modp). Since g has multiplicative order p−1, that order divides N−1. This proves the other condition.[ref]

Euclid's lemma (p∣ab⟹p∣a or p∣b)

Words: 263
Number theory OurBigBook.com
If a prime number p divides a product ab of integers a,b, then p divides a or b (possibly both):
p∣ab⟹p∣a or p∣b.
(90)
For example, 5∣6⋅10 and 5∣10. The hypothesis that p is a prime number matters: 6∣2⋅3, although six divides neither factor. When p does not divide a, the greatest common divisor of p and a is one; multiply Bézout's identity up+va=1 by b to see that p∣b. Repeated application makes this the uniqueness step in the fundamental theorem of arithmetic. [ref].
For a completely computed example, 7∣20⋅21 because 20⋅21=420=7⋅60, while 20=7⋅2+6 shows that seven does not divide twenty. Bézout's identity 3⋅7−20=1 becomes, after multiplication by 21,
21=3⋅7⋅21−20⋅21=7⋅63−7⋅60=7⋅3.
(91)
The two terms on the right are divisible by seven, which explicitly recovers the forced divisibility of the second factor. Both alternatives can hold: 7∣14⋅21, and seven divides both 14 and 21.
In fact the property characterizes prime numbers among the integers greater than one. If c is a composite number, choose c=ab with 1<a,b<c; then c∣ab, but c divides neither a nor b. For several factors, repeated application of Euclid's lemma says that a prime number dividing their product divides at least one factor. In a product of prime numbers, that factor must equal it, because a prime number has no other prime factor. This is what prevents a different collection of prime factors from representing the same positive integer in the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.
Book VII, Proposition 30 of Euclid's Elements states the result in terms of a prime number measuring a product; its proof uses coprimality and ratios. The calculation using Bézout's identity above is a modern way to explain the same divisibility statement. [ref]

Fermat little theorem (ap−1≡1(modp))

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Number theory OurBigBook.com
For a prime number p and an integer a not divisible by p, Fermat's little theorem states the modular congruence
ap−1≡1(modp)(p∤a).
(99)
Equivalently, for every integer a, including a<0 and multiples of p,
ap≡a(modp).
(100)
The first formulation follows from the second by multiplying by a modular multiplicative inverse of a. Conversely, multiply the first by a when p∤a; when p∣a, both sides of the second are zero modulo p. The divisibility condition in the first formulation is essential.[ref]
For p=7, 36=729=7⋅104+1, so 36≡1(mod7) and 37≡3(mod7). Also (−2)6=64≡1(mod7), while 76≡0(mod7): a zero residue class cannot satisfy the first formulation. It does satisfy 77≡7≡0(mod7). A failure at a zero residue class therefore says nothing against a candidate's being a prime number.
The prime number p=2 is included. Its only nonzero residue class is one: every odd integer a satisfies a2−1=a≡1(mod2). Every integer also satisfies a2≡a(mod2), because a(a−1) is even. Testing the first formulation with an even integer would violate its hypothesis.
The useful surprise is that every nonzero residue class returns to one at the same exponent p−1, although its shortest return can be earlier. This gives exponent reduction for units: for a nonnegative integer k, ak≡akmod(p−1)(modp) when p∤a. It also computes a modular multiplicative inverse as ap−2 modulo p, including p=2. Repeated squaring makes these modular exponentiations practical.
In group theory, the nonzero residue classes form the multiplicative group of integers modulo n with n=p, of group order p−1. Lagrange's theorem says that the multiplicative order of a divides p−1, giving the guaranteed return. Euler's theorem extends this to a general integer modulus n, using the units and Euler's totient function φ(n); the Carmichael function gives the least common return exponent for all units. A nonzero residue class modulo a composite number need not be a unit.
Leonhard Euler's paper presented in 1732 and published in 1738 states a historical formulation: Theorem 1 says that powers with exponent n−1 leave zero or one upon division by a prime number n. The preceding discussion states the difference-of-powers version and explicitly says that he does not have its proof.[ref]

Nonzero residue permutation (x↦ax(modp))

Words: 297
Fermat little theorem OurBigBook.com
For a prime number p and p∤a, multiplication by a gives a permutation of the p−1 nonzero residue classes. For a=3 modulo seven, the representatives 1,2,3,4,5,6 map to 3,6,2,5,1,4: the same collection in a different order. Repeating this permutation from one visits all six representatives before returning.
For a=2 modulo seven, the permutation cycles are instead (1,2,4) and (3,6,5). The powers of two visit only the permutation cycle containing one, so their multiplicative order is three. Both permutation cycles return after three steps; applying the permutation six times still fixes every nonzero residue class. Fermat's little theorem guarantees a return at six, not that every base visits every nonzero residue class.
More generally, every permutation cycle of this map has length equal to the multiplicative order of a: starting at a nonzero residue class x, a return means akx≡x(modp), and its modular multiplicative inverse allows cancellation of x. Thus the p−1 nonzero residue classes split into equal-length permutation cycles, which also explains the divisibility of the multiplicative order into p−1.
The product argument gives a short proof outline. Since multiplication by a is a permutation of the nonzero residue classes,
∏r=1p−1​r≡∏r=1p−1​(ar)=ap−1∏r=1p−1​r(modp).
(101)
Every factor is a unit, so their product has a modular multiplicative inverse and can be cancelled. This leaves ap−1≡1(modp). The whole argument works for p=2, where the product is just one.[ref]

Fermat test example

Fermat little theorem OurBigBook.com
For the Fermat primality test, a passing base satisfies an−1≡1(modn). Passing proves only this modular congruence, not that n is a prime number. An odd composite number that passes a coprime base is a Fermat pseudoprime to that base. A Carmichael number passes every coprime base, so even testing all the units would not certify that n is a prime number. [ref]
This small table uses only the bases 2,3,5,11, each reduced modulo n first. A numeric entry is an−1modn: one passes, while any other numeric entry gives a Fermat witness. A "factor" entry records a proper greatest common divisor and stops before modular exponentiation. The prime/composite classification is independently established by trial division or the displayed prime factorization, not by the passing entries. These four bases are illustrative, with no asserted universal coverage or error probability.

The qualification "coprime" is therefore crucial even for a Carmichael number.
The Fermat primality test is useful because a Fermat witness can prove compositeness using repeated squaring without finding a factor. Its failure to certify a passing candidate motivates stronger primality testing methods such as the Miller-Rabin primality test.

Greedy Egyptian fraction expansion
Words: 138
Egyptian fraction OurBigBook.com
For a positive proper residual fraction n/d, with 0<n<d, choose q=⌈d/n⌉, append the unit fraction 1/q, and replace the residual by (nq−d)/(dq) in lowest terms. This is a greedy algorithm: the chosen unit fraction is the largest one not exceeding the residual.
The inequalities q−1<d/n≤q imply 0≤nq−d<n. Thus the numerator of the reduced residual strictly decreases while positive, proving algorithm termination by a nonnegative-integer loop variant. The loop invariant is that the accumulated sum plus the residual is the original rational number. Since q≥2 and n/d<1/(q−1), the new residual is less than 1/(q(q−1))≤1/q. If it remains positive, its next chosen denominator is therefore strictly greater than q; this expansion also satisfies the distinct-denominator convention. The proof does not bound the denominators by the input's fixed-width range. Arbitrary-precision arithmetic, checked conversion, or a different representable expansion can therefore be necessary in code.

Modular multiplicative inverse (a−1(modn))

Words: 284 Articles: 3
Number theory OurBigBook.com
For integers a and n>1, a modular multiplicative inverse is a congruence class b satisfying ab≡1(modn). It exists exactly when gcd(a,n)=1. Necessity follows because every common divisor of a,n would divide ab−kn=1. Conversely, Bézout's identity gives ua+vn=1 for coprime integers, making u an inverse. This is the basic bridge from greatest common divisor calculations to reversible modular arithmetic.
For example, 5⋅7−2⋅17=1, so 5−1≡7(mod17). The modular congruence 5x≡3(mod17) therefore has the unique solution class x≡21≡4(mod17). Multiplication by 5 sends all seventeen residue classes to different classes; multiplying by 7 reverses it. The inverse criterion and its algorithmic construction are presented in Ankur Moitra, MIT 18.200, 2024, modular inverses and Euclid's algorithm.
By contrast, 5 has no modular inverse modulo 15. Its products have only residues 0,5,10. Consequently 5x≡3(mod15) has no solution, while 5x≡10(mod15) has five solution classes, x≡2,5,8,11,14. Dividing by a noninvertible residue would discard this distinction. In a prime field Fp​, every nonzero residue is invertible; a general integer modulus instead gives a quotient ring that can have zero divisors.

Number theory OurBigBook.com
For an integer n>1, the Carmichael function λ(n) is the exponent of a finite group for the unit group U(n)=(Z/nZ)×: the least positive integer m for which
am≡1(modn)for every a with gcd(a,n)=1.
(102)
Here the greatest common divisor condition selects the units. Euler's totient function φ(n) counts them; the Carmichael function gives their least common return exponent.[ref]
Modulo eight, the units are 1,3,5,7, and their squares are all congruent to one. Their multiplicative orders are 1,2,2,2, so λ(8)=2 although φ(8)=4. Modulo fifteen, the units 1,2,4,7,8,11,13,14 have multiplicative orders 1,4,2,4,4,2,4,2. For example, the powers of two return through 1,2,4,8,1. Thus λ(15)=4 although φ(15)=8; the multiplicative order of four is only two.
The three quantities are related by
λ(n)=lcm1≤a<ngcd(a,n)=1​​ordn​(a),ordn​(a)∣λ(n)∣φ(n).

A common return exponent must be a multiple of every multiplicative order, hence of their least common multiple. Conversely, that least common multiple makes every unit return to one. Lagrange's theorem makes each multiplicative order divide the group order φ(n), proving the final divisibility. The Carmichael function applies to all units at once, while the multiplicative order concerns a chosen unit.
For the prime factorization n=∏i=1r​piei​​ with distinct prime numbers pi​ and ei​≥1, the formulas are
λ(n)=lcm(λ(p1e1​​),…,λ(prer​​)),λ(pe)=pe−1(p−1)(p an odd prime),
(104)
λ(2e)=⎩⎨⎧​1,2,2e−2,​e=1,e=2,e≥3.​
(105)
These are least common multiples, rather than products: λ(15)=lcm(2,4)=4. The convention λ(1)=1 handles the trivial case separately.[ref]
The Chinese remainder theorem for unit groups explains the least common multiple: a power returns to one in every prime power component exactly when it is a multiple of each component's exponent of a finite group. For an odd prime power, the unit group is a cyclic group of group order pe−1(p−1). For e≥3, the unit group modulo 2e is a direct product of groups C2​×C2e−2​, generated by the classes of −1 and five, so its exponent of a finite group is 2e−2.[ref]
This gives a uniform reduction for modular exponentiation: for a unit a and a nonnegative integer k, reduce k modulo λ(n). For example, 21001≡2(mod15) because 1001≡1(mod4). The unit hypothesis matters: 32≡1(mod8), but 22≡1(mod8). Computing the formula assumes the prime factorization is available. The same common-exponent viewpoint explains Carmichael numbers: a composite number n passes the Fermat primality test for every unit base exactly when λ(n)∣n−1. For example, λ(561)=lcm(2,10,16)=80∣560.

Number theory OurBigBook.com
For coprime integers a,n with n>1, the multiplicative order is the least positive integer d such that
d=ordn​(a),ad≡1(modn).

It counts the distinct powers in the cyclic subgroup generated by the congruence class of a. Thus it is an order of a group element in the unit group (Z/nZ)×.[ref]
For example, the modular exponentiation 2kmod7, starting at k=0, produces 1,2,4,1,2,4,…. The first return to one takes three steps, so ord7​(2)=3. Starting at the congruence class three and repeatedly multiplying by two instead gives 3,6,5,3,…: these are the other three units modulo seven, outside the cyclic subgroup generated by two.
Euler's theorem guarantees a return to one at exponent φ(n), where φ is Euler's totient function. Thus the multiplicative order exists for every unit.[ref] In fact,
ordn​(a)∣φ(n).
(107)
By Lagrange's theorem, the size of the cyclic subgroup divides the size of the unit group, which is Euler's totient function. For two modulo seven, this is 3∣6; the multiplicative order need not equal Euler's totient function. If a≡1(modn), its multiplicative order is one.
The coprime integers hypothesis is necessary: if ad=1+kn, any common divisor of a and n divides one. For instance, powers of two modulo eight give 1,2,4,0,0,…, with no positive-exponent return to one. This sequence eventually settles, but two has no multiplicative order modulo eight.

Euclidean algorithm

Words: 383 Articles: 4
Number theory OurBigBook.com
For positive integers a,b, the Euclidean algorithm repeatedly performs division with remainder: write a=qb+r with 0≤r<b, then replace (a,b) by (b,r) until the second entry is zero. The final nonzero entry is their greatest common divisor. A remainder preserves the set of common divisors: an integer divides a and b exactly when it divides b and a−qb. The positive remainders strictly decrease, so the calculation terminates.
The complete calculation for 252 and 198 is
2521985436​=1⋅198+54,=3⋅54+36,=1⋅36+18,=2⋅18+0.​
(115)
Hence gcd(252,198)=18. The fraction 252/198 reduces to 14/11 by dividing numerator and denominator by that common factor. The same remainder calculation has a geometric interpretation: remove squares from a 252-by-198 rectangle, then repeat on the remaining strip. Each division step records how many equal squares fit and the width of the new strip.
The procedure does more than test individual divisors. Each step replaces the whole common-divisor problem by a smaller equivalent one. Euclid's Book VII, Proposition 2 describes the corresponding repeated-subtraction construction; batching those subtractions into division with remainder gives the present formulation. [ref]

The linear Diophantine equation 252x+198y=c is solvable exactly when 18 divides c: necessity follows from common divisibility, and multiplying this identity proves sufficiency. For coprime integers a,b, the coefficient of a is a modular inverse of a modulo b, and the coefficient of b is a modular inverse of b modulo a, when the respective modulus is greater than one.

A positive integer is a sum of two integer squares exactly when every prime factor congruent to 3 modulo 4 has even exponent in its prime factorization.

Brahmagupta-Fibonacci identity

Words: 29
Sum of two squares theorem OurBigBook.com
The identity (a2+b2)(c2+d2)=(ac−bd)2+(ad+bc)2 shows that a product of two sums of two squares is another sum of two squares. It follows by multiplying Gaussian integers and taking their squared absolute values.

Congruence lattice proof of the prime sum of two squares (Λ={(a,b)∈Z2:b≡ua(modp)})

Words: 59
Sum of two squares theorem OurBigBook.com
If u2≡−1(modp), this lattice has basis (1,u),(0,p) and covolume p. The Minkowski convex body theorem applied to a disk of squared radius strictly between 4p/π and 2p gives a nonzero lattice vector with 0<a2+b2<2p. The congruence makes its squared length divisible by p, forcing a2+b2=p. The strict radius bounds avoid assuming the critical-volume form of Minkowski's theorem.
